subject: Accounting
title: Capital Gains Tax
description: A quick win: understand Capital Gains Tax.

hook.text: You buy stock for $1,000 and sell it for $5,000. The $4,000 profit gets taxed—but how much?

buildup.text: Capital gains tax applies to profits from selling assets like stocks, real estate, or businesses.

discovery.text: Hold the asset over a year and the tax rate drops. Short-term gains are taxed like regular income.

twist.text: Billionaires often pay lower tax rates than employees because most of their wealth is in long-term gains.

climax.text: The debate over capital gains rates sits at the heart of tax fairness discussions worldwide.

punchline.text: Patience pays—literally. Hold longer, pay less tax.

quiz.question: Why are long-term capital gains taxed at lower rates?

details.summary: Capital gains tax is levied on profits from selling assets like stocks, real estate, and businesses. Long-term gains (held over a year) are typically taxed at lower rates than ordinary income, creating both investment incentives and equity debates.
details.whyItMatters: Capital gains taxation shapes investment behavior, wealth accumulation, and inequality. Its preferential rates compared to income tax are among the most debated features of modern tax systems.
takeaways: Capital gains tax applies to the profit from selling an asset — the difference between purchase and sale price
Long-term gains (assets held over one year) receive lower tax rates than short-term gains
The lower rate for long-term gains is designed to encourage long-term investment

faq.question: What qualifies as a capital gain?
faq.answer: A capital gain occurs when you sell an asset for more than you paid for it. This includes stocks, bonds, real estate, and business interests. If you bought stock for $5,000 and sold it for $8,000, your capital gain is $3,000. This gain is taxable in the year you sell.

faq.question: Why are long-term capital gains taxed at lower rates than regular income?
faq.answer: The lower rate encourages long-term investment rather than short-term speculation. Supporters argue this promotes economic growth and job creation. Critics counter that it primarily benefits wealthy investors and contributes to inequality since most capital gains accrue to high-income individuals.
